title: A Loop You Can Run in a Millisecond: A Scheduler on a Test Clock, and Why Its Time Is an Integer

questions.question: A loop is tested by running it for ten seconds and waiting. What does a scheduler on a test clock change?
options: It makes the loop faster on the robot
It removes the need for tests
It takes the next event, sets the clock to its time and runs it
questions.explanation: Ten seconds of events run without waiting. Ten minutes of a 1 kHz loop was 600001 ticks and no waiting.

questions.question: A 100 Hz sensor and a 10 Hz logger run for ten seconds, with the start and end both ticks. How many times does each run?
Why does a tick every 0.1 s up to 0.3 s run 4 times with integer nanoseconds and 3 times with doubles added up?
options: It is a bug in the loop
0.1 is not exact in binary, and three of them make 0.30000000000000004, which is later than 0.3
questions.explanation: The last tick is lost. Time is kept as int64 nanoseconds, as in lesson 03-05.

questions.question: The sensor and the logger are both due at 100 ms. The first version of the scheduler ran the logger first. Why?
options: Ties were broken by queue order, and a repeating task queues its next tick as it finishes the last
questions.explanation: The slower task's older event won. The fix is to break ties by registration order.

questions.question: A task registers another task while the scheduler is calling it. What must the scheduler have done first?
options: Copied the entry's period and task out of the vector
questions.explanation: Adding an entry can move the vector and the function being run. A task at +5 ms ran in the same run, and one at +500 ms waited.

questions.question: Which problem can a scheduler on a test clock not show?
options: A race between two threads, or a task that overruns its period
questions.explanation: Tasks take no time and run one at a time. It models when things happen, not how they overlap.
